newsitem.title: USA: Wall St to look for trouble ahead in Q1 earnings.
newsitem.headline: Wall St to look for trouble ahead in Q1 earnings.

text.p: Wall Street will scour first-quarter earnings reports for signs that stocks could lose further momentum, aware of the impact of the strong dollar and the potential for a slowing economy.

High-profile companies such as Eastman Kodak Co and AT&T Corp, and lesser-known names such as IDEXX Laboratories Inc, have already fired warning shots heading into the profit-reporting period that gets under way in earnest during mid-April.

To be sure, Wall Street expects the headline first-quarter earnings-per-share numbers to be strong for most companies. But many market players will be keying on management indications of weakness in subsequent quarters, analysts said.

"I think earnings will be OK, so that may not be the thing that really drives stocks in the next handful of weeks," said Charlie Crane, chief market strategist at Key Asset Management. "Interest rates will be the No.1 determinant, as well as the tone of the outlooks described by management when they report their earnings."

Wall Street expects operating earnings from the Standard & Poor's 500 companies to show an average year-over-year rise of 12.1 percent in the first quarter, which ends March 31, said Chuck Hill, director of research at First Call. That comes after a 11.8 percent gain in the fourth quarter of 1996.

Still, the strength of the U.S. dollar -- which lowers U.S. companies' foreign sales in dollar terms -- coupled with a slowing economy resulting from rising interest rates will likely weigh on corporate profits, if not in the first quarter, then in subsequent periods, analysts said.
"By and large the nature of earnings are going to be that they will be more tending to disappoint than to surprise on the upside," said Charles Pradillo, market analyst at Cowen and Co.
Several stocks have recently witnessed Wall Street's lack of tolerance for earnings disappointments.

Kodak fell 9-1/4 points on Friday and another 2-5/8 on Monday after saying lower prices and a stronger dollar meant its January and February sales were essentially flat compared with the first two months of last year. The stock recovered 1-1/4 to 77-5/8 in early afternoon trading on Tuesday.
AT&T's shares were rocked earlier this month after it said costs of new ventures would trim its 1997 earnings.
IDEXX Laboratories shrank 63 percent on Monday after it said it expected its first-quarter earnings to fall significantly below analysts' forecasts.
The overall carnage in high-technology stocks in past weeks are an indication of Wall Street's earnings sentiments.

Analysts expect earnings in the technology group, which includes semiconductors, computers, software and communications hardware, to rise by a solid 28 percent in the first quarter, according to First Call.
But the Nasdaq Composite index, the high-technology barometer, has fallen 10 percent from its January 22 peak as investors anticipate a slowdown in the group.

"The big problems have been in high-tech companies that have been reporting earnings increase that just don't match the high expectations of investors," said Jim Solloway, director of research at Argus Research.
The energy sector is expected to post a 19 percent rise in earnings, but the group's profits are decelerating after a 25 percent rise for all of 1996, First Call said.

Financial companies are seen reporting an 11 percent rise in earnings, led by banks. "I think they're going to continue to show good margin growth in their bottom lines," said Bruce Bittles, market strategist at J.C. Bradford.
But brokerage firms face tough comparisions against the first quarter of 1996 amid a slowdown in initial and secondary stock offerings, analysts said.

Basic material stocks, such as paper, chemical and steel producers, are seen starting to pull out of a cyclical downturn. Their earnings are expected to be down on average 12 percent in the first quarter, but that comes after a 29 percent drop in the fourth quarter of last year.
